title: Recover Per Operation Without Losing Valid State

blocks.text: The Position of try Determines Which Operation Is Abandoned

If try surrounds an entire session, a failure in one order can end the whole traversal. If try is inside the loop and surrounds the current order, a catch can handle that failure and then allow the loop to visit the next order. Neither policy is automatic or always correct: decide which unit of work may be abandoned based on the requirement.

blocks.question: Which test shows that processing continues with another order after rejecting one?
options: A session containing only valid inputs.
A session with a valid input, an invalid input, and another valid input, also checking the last one.
A single invalid input that displays a message.
blocks.explanation: Displaying the message proves that the rejection was reported. The later valid operation proves that processing resumed from a known state.

blocks.text: Do Not Update the Summary Before the Operation Succeeds

If you increment aceptados before calling a function that might fail, the counter can record a rejected order as accepted. If you add minutes only after obtaining a valid result, there is no need to undo an update that never happened. This ordering rule also applies to error codes; exceptions do not change the meaning of the summary.

Correctness criteria. For {0,11,2,-1,5}, three orders are accepted, two are rejected, and the total is 20 minutes. The rejected inputs, 11 and -1, are identified. In the reference, the final summary is 3:2:20. {} produces 0:0:0; {11,-1} produces 0:2:0; {11,2} produces 1:1:7. The field order is accepted:rejected:minutes; another labeled format is valid. The rejection-then-valid case must test continued processing and preservation of the summary.

The try/catch handles one order at a time inside the loop. Only after minutes are obtained does success affect the summary; a rejection contributes no normal result.
